family: Hebrew-keyed ring-letter alphabets (Brillenbuchstaben). Printed with the Celestial and Malachim scripts in Agrippa's De occulta philosophia III.30.
summary: Transitus Fluvii, 'the Passing of the River', is a 22-letter alphabet keyed one-for-one to the Hebrew letters, of the ring-ended kind scholars call Brillenbuchstaben. Agrippa printed it in De occulta philosophia III.30 (1533) with the Celestial and Malachim scripts, as a writing found among the Hebrews which, in the 1651 English, 'they call the passing through the River'; he names no source. Scholars report that it had already appeared in Abraham de Balmes's Hebrew-Latin grammar Mikneh Avram / Peculium Abrae (Venice: Bomberg, 1523), under a Hebrew name reported as Ketav ever ha-nahar, 'script of Beyond-the-River'. Macfarlane (2025), following Campanini, dates the reading of it as the script Abraham used when he crossed the Euphrates to Panteo (1530).

firstAttestation.notes: Macfarlane (JHI 2025) is reported to call this the first Brillenbuchstaben alphabet printed in Europe (paraphrase; from the abstract and snippets the researcher read). The Rylands blog is reported to give its Hebrew name as Ketav ever ha-nahar ('Script beyond the River'), to describe it as made of charaktêres, and to say that de Balmes presented it, in a grammar rather than a magical work, as an example of the alphabets derived from the original 'Ashuri' script. The Latin label 'scriptura transitus fluuii' is reported from this book in the scholarship that follows Campanini. Agrippa III.30 (1533) is the most influential printing, but it comes ten years after de Balmes. Nobody in this research saw the page; a digitised copy is reported (identifier withdrawn as unverified). Ring-letter alphabets keyed to Hebrew are reported in medieval Jewish manuscripts (Macfarlane; Bohak), but no manuscript copy of this alphabet earlier than 1523 is identified here.

transmission.work: Mikneh Avram / Peculium Abrae (Venice: Daniel Bomberg)
transmission.author: Abraham de Balmes
transmission.what: First printing, as reported by Macfarlane 2025, Peterson and the Rylands blog (not seen). Shown in a Hebrew grammar as Ketav ever ha-nahar, one of the scripts derived from Ashuri; the Latin side is reported to label it 'scriptura transitus fluuii'. Campanini argues that this terse label, whose Talmudic background Christian readers did not know, set off the later misreadings (as summarised by Macfarlane).

transmission.author: Geoffroy Tory
transmission.what: Wikipedia says Tory prints this alphabet as 'Lettres Chaldaiques' at f. 76v. The BnF's own image record of the 'Lettres chaldaïques et lettres goffes' gives f. 73r, and says Tory presents the Chaldaic letters as the signs the Hebrews used in Moses's time. The folio and the identification are both unchecked.

transmission.date: 1530 (the month 'April' is reported but not confirmed)
transmission.author: Giovanni Agostino Panteo (Pantheus)
transmission.what: Reported (Chioli; Wikipedia) to print it, under a Latin heading naming it the writing of the transitus fluuii, in a bilingual Hebrew/Latin passage that assigns it to Abraham, as Hebrew to Moses and Panteo's own 'Enochian' to Enoch. Macfarlane, following Campanini, makes Panteo the first of many to read it as the script Abraham used when he crossed the Euphrates. Wikipedia's locator 'pp. 545-46' cannot be the foliation of the 1530 quarto and probably refers to a later reprint, not identified. A second-hand blog report (Pelling, Cipher Mysteries, 2009, via the malachim research file) says Panteo's 'transitus fluvii' is a conglomeration of all three of Agrippa's alphabets; if so, Panteo's plate is not simply this alphabet. The plate was not seen.

transmission.date: 1533 (colophon July 1533 per the Wellcome catalogue; place given as Cologne, printer probably J. Soter, though Adams suspected Basel, per Eton College's catalogue; all as reported, not re-checked)
transmission.author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
transmission.what: Book III chapter 30; in the 1651 English, 'CHAP. XXX. Another manner of making Characters, delivered by Cabalists.' (verified, EEBO-TCP A26565 (Wing A789), p. 439). Agrippa lists the scripts he finds 'Amongst the Hebrews' in order: the most ancient, which Moses and the prophets used; 'those letters which they use at this day', instituted by Esdras (Ezra); the Celestial; the Malachim; and 'another, which they call the passing through the River' (all 1651 wording, verified). For 1533 the three alphabets are reported as one woodcut with Transitus Fluvii at the bottom (stock-image caption only; not seen). In 1651 they are three separate tables on pp. 439, 440 and 441 (verified). Perrone Compagni's critical edition (Brill, 1992) is reported to have the passage at p. 491 (per Wikipedia; unchecked). Agrippa names no source; the pointer to de Balmes is reported to be Peterson's annotation.

transmission.work: Three Books of Occult Philosophy (London: Printed by R.W. for Gregory Moule, 1651; Wing A789), translated by 'J.F.' (the EEBO-TCP record says 'The translator is probably John French. Cf. DNB.')
transmission.author: Agrippa, tr. J.F.
transmission.what: English text of Book III ch. XXX, verified in EEBO-TCP A26565 (Wing A789): the text (p. 439) calls it 'the passing through the River', and the table on p. 441 is headed 'The writing called the passing of the River.' The table labels exactly 22 signs with Hebrew letter-names, in three rows of 7, 8 and 7 running right to left (Aleph, Cheth and Ain at the right of their rows), with no numbers and no final forms. TCP does not transcribe the glyphs ('in non-Latin alphabet'); the page image is EEBO image tcp:52070:236. Whether the 1651 cuts copy the 1533 forms faithfully is unchecked. Peterson is reported to warn that the J.F. translation adds errors (not re-checked), so check its forms against 1533.

transmission.work: Campanini, 'The Quest for the Holiest Alphabet in the Renaissance'; Macfarlane, 'Written in the Stars? Alphabets and Angels in Early Modern Europe'
transmission.author: Saverio Campanini; Kirsten Macfarlane
transmission.what: The modern scholarly reconstruction, known here only from descriptions, abstracts and snippets. Campanini (esp. pp. 211-15, per the volume's description) traces the alphabet from de Balmes's grammar through its Christian misreading and its spread from Venice into north-western Europe. Macfarlane builds on him to show how Brillenbuchstaben came to be treated as star-derived alphabets authored by angels.

claims.claim: The alphabet was first printed in Abraham de Balmes's Mikneh Avram / Peculium Abrae (Venice: Bomberg, 1523), ten years before Agrippa.
claims.evidence: Reported by three scholarly witnesses: Macfarlane 2025 (who is reported to call it the first Brillenbuchstaben alphabet printed in Europe), Peterson's note at Agrippa III.30 (sig. B6v) and the Rylands blog (Ketav ever ha-nahar). Neither the researcher nor the fact-checker saw the page, and the three sources were not re-opened in the fact-check.

Rylands Blog, 'Speaking to angels' part II (2022)

claims.claim: Agrippa presents it as a writing of the Hebrews ('which they call the passing through the River') among the Cabalists' characters, without naming any source or inventor.
claims.evidence: Verified in the 1651 English (EEBO-TCP A26565 (Wing A789), p. 439). Agrippa introduces it among the 'fashions of Characters' he finds 'Amongst the Hebrews', as 'another, which they call the passing through the River', and names no source, inventor or book. The 1533 Latin is known here only as quoted by Chioli (not seen). Some web pages say Agrippa attributed it to de Balmes; his text does not. The link to de Balmes is reported to come from Peterson's editorial note.
sources: J.F. translation, 1651, Book III ch. XXX, p. 439 (EEBO-TCP A26565 (Wing A789))

claims.claim: Agrippa invented the alphabet (the 'creator' named in Wikipedia's infobox and in hobby sites).
claims.evidence: It is reported in print in 1523 (de Balmes) and 1530 (Panteo), before 1533, and Agrippa himself gives it as a writing that 'they call' by this name (1651 wording, verified). Agrippa is its best-known transmitter, not its documented author.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Transitus Fluvii' (which itself lists the earlier printings)

claims.claim: De Balmes presented the alphabet as one of the scripts derived from the original 'Ashuri' (square) script, in a grammar.
claims.evidence: Rylands blog, part II, as reported by the researcher. A single secondary source; not re-checked.
sources: Rylands Blog, 'Speaking to angels' part II (2022)

claims.claim: Christian readers misread de Balmes's terse label 'transitus fluuii' because they did not know its Talmudic background, and this produced the 'transfluvial alphabet' of Abraham.
claims.evidence: This is Saverio Campanini's reconstruction (2014, pp. 211–15), as summarised by Macfarlane 2025 and by the Glagolitic-characters article in Redalyc. I could not read the chapter. Which Talmudic passage he means is not stated in what I saw; the Talmud's discussion of ketav Ivri and ketav Ashurit (b. Sanhedrin 21b–22a) is the obvious candidate, but that is my inference.
sources: Campanini, 'The Quest for the Holiest Alphabet in the Renaissance' (2014)

claims.claim: The alphabet was entrusted to Abraham, as Hebrew was to Moses and the 'Enochian' to Enoch.
claims.evidence: Panteo's claim in Voarchadumia (1530), as reported by Wikipedia and Chioli (not re-checked). Report it as 'Panteo assigns it to Abraham'. Note the second-hand report (Pelling 2009) that Panteo's plate mixes signs from all three of Agrippa's alphabets.

claims.claim: The name refers to Abraham's crossing of the Euphrates.
claims.evidence: Macfarlane 2025 (paraphrase): many readers, starting with Panteo, took the transfluvial alphabet for the one Abraham used when he crossed the Euphrates. The idea rests on the ʿIvri ('Hebrew') = 'one from beyond the River' etymology: Joshua 24:2-3; Genesis 14:13 with Genesis Rabbah 42:8 and Rashi; the Septuagint's rendering of Abram 'the Hebrew' as the one who crosses (peratēs).

claims.claim: The name refers to the Jews' crossing of the Euphrates on their return from the Babylonian captivity to rebuild the Temple.
claims.evidence: A modern suggestion in Wikipedia ('may refer'), with no early source. It is not in Agrippa (1651 text verified), and not in de Balmes or Panteo as far as the researcher found. Omniglot repeats it but is not usable for history (house rule).

claims.claim: The name refers to the crossing of the river Chebar.
claims.evidence: Blavatsky's Theosophical Glossary (1892), entry 'Fluvii Transitus', as transcribed by Teopedia. It is a nineteenth-century theosophical gloss.

claims.claim: Hebrew ʿIvri means 'one from the other side (ʿever) of the River', so 'Hebrews' are 'those who crossed'.
claims.evidence: This is one traditional etymology, not a settled one. Genesis Rabbah 42:8 gives three readings: R. Judah says the whole world stood on one side and Abraham on the other; R. Nehemiah says it means descended from Eber; and the Rabbis say he came from beyond the River. Rashi adopts 'from the other side of the River'. The Septuagint renders Abram 'the Hebrew' at Gen 14:13 as ho peratēs, 'the one who crosses / migrant'. The three opinions in Genesis Rabbah 42:8 agree with the fact-checker's knowledge of the text; not re-checked against an edition in this pass.

claims.claim: Agrippa had the alphabet in his c. 1510 draft of De occulta philosophia.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia says the book was 'written around 1510'. Trithemius's reply to the draft is dated 'From our Monastery of Peapolis, the 8. day of April, An. M. D. X.' (1651 front matter, verified in EEBO-TCP A26565 (Wing A789)), so the draft existed by then. The SEP is reported to say the draft was reworked and enlarged for 1533. No evidence was found that III.30's alphabets were in the draft. Since de Balmes's 1523 printing is the earliest known, date Agrippa's use to 1533 only.
sources: Trithemius to Agrippa, 8 April 1510, 1651 front matter (EEBO-TCP A26565 (Wing A789))

claims.claim: Agrippa's tables set the letters out right to left, with Aleph at the right, as in Hebrew.
claims.evidence: Verified for 1651 (EEBO-TCP A26565 (Wing A789), p. 441): the three rows of labels read 'Zain Vau He Daleth Gimel Beth Aleph', 'Samech Nun Mem Lamed Caph Iod Teth Cheth', 'Tau Schin Res Kuph Zade Pe Ain'. For 1533, a Source Library transcription (reported, not re-checked) reads the first row 'Cheth Zain Vau He Daleth Gimel Beth Aleph'. This shows how the table is laid out, not how the script was written: no text written in this alphabet is cited. Wikipedia's statement that the script is written right to left is unsourced.
sources: Source Library, 'agrippa von nettesheim 3 alphabets' (as reported)

letters.name: Aleph
letters.form: NOT DESCRIBED. No facsimile of any printing could be viewed by the researcher or the fact-checker, and no source describes this letter in words, so no form is given; a guessed form would be worse than a gap. The only reported trait is the family one: Brillenbuchstaben carry small rings ('Brillen') at stroke-ends. Which strokes of this letter carry rings, and how many, is unknown. Trace it from one named plate: the 1651 English table, p. 441 (EEBO image tcp:52070:236), row 1 from the top, 1st sign from the right, labelled 'Aleph' (position inferred from the order of the labels in the TCP transcription); or the 1533 woodcut (reported as the bottom alphabet of III.30); or de Balmes 1523 (sig. B6v, reported).
letters.note: Value and order follow the Hebrew alphabet, which the table follows one-for-one. The numeric value is the standard Hebrew one; the 1651 table prints names only, with no numbers and no final forms. The label 'Aleph' is verified in the 1651 table (EEBO-TCP A26565 (Wing A789), p. 441). A Source Library transcription, reported by the researcher as of the 1533 woodcut, gives the same spelling (not re-checked). Peterson's CC-BY 4.0 'Transitus Fluvii' font is reported to follow de Balmes 1523, not Agrippa, so its forms may differ from both 1533 and 1651 (not re-checked).

links.relation: Its 22 signs stand one-for-one for the Hebrew letters, in Hebrew order, labelled with the Hebrew letter-names (1651 table, verified). De Balmes is reported to present it as a script derived from Ashuri, the square Hebrew script (Rylands blog).
Printed with it in Agrippa III.30. In 1651 the 'Celestiall writing' table stands on p. 439 (verified). In 1533 it is reported as the top row of a single woodcut (stock-image caption; not seen).

Agrippa's preceding chapter, III.29 ('Of the Characters and Seals of spirits'), prints the characters 'which Peter Apponus notes, as delivered by Honorius of Thebes' (1651 wording, verified), known today as the Theban alphabet.
After the three alphabets, the same chapter III.30 goes on to the twenty-seven Hebrew letters in three classes and the 'nine Chambers' (1651, pp. 441-442, verified).

Bohak (2011) traces the ring-ended charaktêres of Jewish magic to those of Graeco-Egyptian magic; the ring-letter alphabets belong to that family. Reported, not re-checked; no letter of this alphabet is traced to a particular ancient sign.

The Talmud's contrast of ketav Ivri (Palaeo-Hebrew, a Phoenician-type script) with ketav Ashurit is a possible 'Talmudic background' to de Balmes's label. This link is the researcher's inference, not Campanini's stated argument.

cautions: Do not say Agrippa invented it, or that Agrippa cites de Balmes. It is reported in print in 1523 and 1530 before Agrippa; the pointer to de Balmes is Peterson's editorial note, not Agrippa's text (1651 text verified: no source named).

All three explanations of the name (Abraham's Euphrates; the return from Babylon; the Chebar) are later interpretations. Report each with its author: Panteo onward, per Macfarlane; modern Wikipedia, unsourced; Blavatsky 1892.

The Hebrew name ever ha-nahar means 'beyond the River', a place, while Latin transitus fluvii means 'the crossing of the river', an act. That shift in sense is the researcher's own observation, offered as a possible reason the label was misread. It is not a quotation of Campanini.

The 'Ivri = one who crossed over' etymology is one of three in Genesis Rabbah 42:8, alongside 'descendant of Eber' and 'he stood on the other side from the whole world'. Present it as a tradition, not a fact of philology.

No letter form here is described or verified. Every glyph must be traced from a named plate (1533 III.30, de Balmes 1523 sig. B6v, or, for cross-checking only, 1651 p. 441), and the page should say which.
The 1651 English calls it 'the passing through the River' in the text (p. 439) but heads the table 'The writing called the passing of the River.' (p. 441). Quote whichever you use with its page.
The 1651 table runs right to left. If the site shows the letters left to right, say that it reverses the plate.

Panteo's 1530 plate may not be this alphabet letter for letter: a second-hand blog report (Pelling 2009) says it mixes signs from all three of Agrippa's alphabets. Do not present Panteo's plate as identical, or draw from it, until it has been compared.
Folio and page numbers taken from Wikipedia (Tory f. 76v, Panteo pp. 545-46, Perrone Compagni p. 491) are unverified. Tory's folio conflicts with the BnF's f. 73r.
Kircher's and Westcott's reproductions are reported second-hand. Duret, Vigenère and Theseus Ambrosius were searched for and NOT confirmed to print this alphabet, so leave them out.

dCode's 'page 441 of Book III' matches the page of the 1651 English edition on which this table stands (EEBO-TCP A26565 (Wing A789) page break 441), so it very probably refers to that edition. It is not a locator for 1533.
